questions.question: Which area receives the largest share of UK public spending?

options.B: Social protection, including state pensions and benefits

questions.why: Social protection is consistently the largest function in HM Treasury PESA spending tables.

questions.question: Roughly what share of the UK's national income (GDP) does total public spending equal in recent years?
questions.why: Total managed expenditure has been around 40-45% of GDP in recent years.

questions.question: Each year, which receives more UK public money?

options.D: Neither; both are funded only by charities

questions.why: Health spending is several times larger than defence spending in PESA.

questions.question: Spending on a service rose 20% in cash terms over ten years. What do you also need to know if it grew in real terms?

options.A: How much prices rose over the period
options.D: Nothing else; cash growth is real growth

questions.why: Real growth is cash growth adjusted for inflation.

questions.question: Which single tax raises the most money for the UK government?
questions.why: Income tax is the largest single source of receipts in OBR and HMRC figures.

questions.question: Which three together raise more than half of UK government receipts?

options.A: Fuel duty, alcohol duty and stamp duty
options.B: Income tax, National Insurance and VAT
options.C: Council tax, business rates and inheritance tax
options.D: Corporation tax, tobacco duty and air passenger duty

questions.why: Income tax, NICs and VAT together make up well over half of receipts.

questions.question: When the government spends more than it receives in a year, how is the gap mainly covered?

options.B: By an automatic extra VAT charge
options.C: By the Bank of England's profits
options.D: It cannot happen; budgets must balance

questions.why: The gap is public sector net borrowing, which is not a tax.

questions.question: Which UK tax is charged on the profits that companies make?
questions.why: Corporation tax is the UK tax on company profits, as described by HMRC.

questions.question: Roughly what share of all income tax is paid by the top 1% of income taxpayers?

options.C: Around a quarter to a third

questions.why: HMRC estimates put the top 1% share of income tax at roughly 25-30%.

questions.question: ONS figures show the poorest fifth of households pay indirect taxes such as VAT that take what share of their disposable income, compared with the richest fifth?
questions.why: ONS Effects of taxes and benefits shows indirect taxes take a higher proportion of income for the poorest fifth.

questions.question: Measured in pounds, which group of households pays the most tax on average?

options.D: All fifths pay the same amount

questions.why: ONS shows the richest fifth pay far more tax in pounds, even though shares of income differ less.

questions.question: 'The top 1% pay 28% of income tax.' What does the 28% describe?

options.B: Their share of all income tax collected
options.C: Their share of the UK population

questions.why: It is a share of total revenue, not a tax rate paid on anyone's income.

questions.question: Which of these is an indirect tax?
questions.why: VAT is paid through prices; ONS treats income tax, NICs and council tax as direct taxes.

questions.question: A chart says households in a group pay 30% of their income in all taxes on average. What does this tell you?

options.A: Every household in the group pays exactly 30%
options.B: Your own income tax rate is 30%
options.C: An average across those households, including direct and indirect taxes
options.D: 30% of all UK tax revenue comes from them

questions.why: A household average across all taxes is neither an individual rate nor a share of revenue.

questions.question: A page shows 'Example: two adults, two children, earning £40,000', with its tax bill. What is this?

options.A: A labelled illustration, not a measured statistic
options.D: The legal definition of a typical household

questions.why: Worked examples are illustrations and must be kept separate from measured figures.

questions.question: In ONS household tax figures, what are 'combined' or total taxes?

options.B: Direct and indirect taxes added together

questions.why: Total taxes are the sum of direct and indirect taxes paid by households.

questions.question: Average pay rose 10% while prices rose 12% over the same period. What happened to pay after inflation?
questions.why: Real pay falls when prices rise faster than cash pay.

questions.question: Employment rose in the years after a new policy started. What does that chart alone show?

options.B: That employment rose, not why it rose
options.D: Employment would have fallen without it

questions.why: A change over time does not by itself show what caused it.

questions.question: The ONS headline employment rate is the share of which group who are in work?

options.A: Everyone in the UK, including children

questions.why: The ONS headline employment rate covers people aged 16 to 64 in any paid work.

questions.question: What is the most common way English households occupy their homes?

options.B: Renting from a council or housing association
options.C: Owning, outright or with a mortgage

questions.why: The English Housing Survey shows around two-thirds of households are owner-occupiers.

questions.question: In England, what is the legal limit for most infant (Key Stage 1) class sizes with one teacher?
questions.why: The infant class size limit in England is 30 pupils per school teacher.

questions.question: A class-size figure is labelled 'England, state-funded primary schools'. What does it describe?
questions.why: Class-size statistics are specific to the nation and school phase stated.

questions.question: Which country do UK residents visit most often on trips abroad?
questions.why: ONS Travel Trends consistently shows Spain as the top destination for UK residents' visits abroad.

questions.question: A survey was not run in 2020 and changed its definitions in 2008. How should a chart show this?

options.B: Join the line smoothly across both
options.C: Show 2020 as a gap and mark 2008 as a break
options.D: Leave out all years before 2008 without saying so

questions.why: Missing years and definition changes should be shown explicitly, not filled or hidden.
